name: Proton Drive
summary: End-to-end encrypted cloud storage from a Swiss provider. Because Proton cannot read your files there is no server-side search inside documents, integrations are thinner, and losing your credentials without recovery loses the data.
best_for: privacy-conscious individuals and businesses that want genuinely end-to-end-encrypted storage from a Swiss provider, ideally as part of the wider Proton suite
skip_if: your workflow lives on deep integrations, shared-drive collaboration and full-text search (mainstream clouds do that better), or you'd never set up account recovery
honest_knock: End-to-end encryption is the point and the price. Because Proton can't read your files, there's no server-side search inside documents. Previews and third-party integrations are more limited than Google Drive or Dropbox, and losing your credentials without recovery set up means losing data — by design. You trade convenience for the mathematical guarantee that nobody, including Proton, can look inside.

pricing.plans_source: hand-curated from the vendor's pricing page
pricing.notes: (read 2026-08-26 over a US connection and re-read 2026-10-16 with USD selected, on proton.me/drive/pricing, Individuals view with yearly billing) Proton Free gives 5 GB. Drive Plus is $3.99 a month for 200 GB, marked 20% off $4.99 and billed at $47.88 every twelve months. Proton Unlimited is $9.99 for 500 GB and folds in the VPN, Mail and Calendar, billed at $119.88 a year. Proton Duo is $14.99 for 2 TB across two users at $179.88 a year, and Proton Family $23.99 for 3 TB and up to six. Teams get Drive Professional at $7.99 per user a month for 1 TB each. The page carries its own currency selector with CHF, EUR and USD, so these are the US default rather than a conversion. The thing worth seeing in that ladder: Drive Plus is the only tier that is storage on its own — every step above it bundles the rest of Proton, so you are buying a suite the moment you need more than 200 GB.

third_party_video.shows: signing in, uploading files, and sharing a password-protected link from the Proton Drive web app

sessions.what: A new free account, used in the web app in Chrome. We uploaded four files we made ourselves with known SHA-256 checksums: a 9.6 KB text note, 1 MB and 8 MB files of random bytes, and a small text file named 'naam met spaties en é.txt' to test spaces and an accented letter. We created a public link for the 1 MB file, opened it in a separate browser that was not signed in to Proton, then downloaded all four files again and compared them byte for byte with the originals.
findings: All four files came back identical: the same size and the same SHA-256 checksum as the originals, and the file name with spaces and an accented letter was unchanged, byte for byte.

The new account started at 2 GB, not 5 GB. A pop-up offered a 3 GB welcome bonus, and after we uploaded files and created a share link the meter showed 5 GB. The same pop-up still said '29 days left to claim' afterwards.

The public link opened for a visitor without a Proton account and offered the file for download. The decryption key is the part of the link after the '#': the same link without it showed a password prompt instead, so a chat app or mail client that cuts off that part leaves the recipient stuck.
Setting an expiry date and a password on a link is available on the free plan; we opened both settings but did not save them.
not_tested: the desktop and mobile apps, sync, photo backup, version history, sharing with another Proton user, and large uploads
sessions.note: Findings as written up after the session; no pass/fail per task was scored.
